submissions.abstract: In previous work by Fel2022, the authors showed that "harmonizing" deep neural networks with human psychophysics to force them to rely on the same visual features as human observers aligned models with human perception while maintaining classification accuracy. Here, we scale up this approach with ClickMe 2.0, a larger and more robust behavioral dataset, and more efficient harmonization methods that make it feasible to align models across the full PyTorch Image Models (TIMM) library. Harmonized models exhibit substantially improved alignment with human visual strategies on ImageNet, which also yields higher correspondence with electrophysiological recordings from macaque visual cortex, and improved robustness against visual perturbations. We release all the harmonized weights as an open resource for the community.

submissions.title: Human-level 3D perception emerges from multi-view learning
submissions.abstract: Here we introduce the first modeling framework that matches human performance on 3D visual tasks. We leverage a novel class of neural networks trained with a visual-spatial objective; given images from different locations within a scene, these models must learn to predict associated spatial information, such as camera position and visual depth. Notably, these visual-spatial data are analogous to sensory cues readily available to humans. We design a zero-shot evaluation approach to determine the performance of these `multi-view' models on a well established 3D perception benchmark, then compare model and human behavior. Our modeling approach is the first to match human accuracy on 3D shape inferences, even without training or fine-tuning on experimental data or images. Remarkably, independent readouts of model responses predict fine-grained measures of human behavior, including error patterns and reaction times, revealing a natural correspondence between model dynamics and human perception. Our findings indicate that human-level 3D perception can emerge from a simple, scalable learning objective over naturalistic visual-spatial data.

submissions.title: Automated recall-to-story matching for memory research
submissions.abstract: Research on memory increasingly relies on paradigms using naturalistic stimuli in which participants freely recall stories or films in their own words. For many analyses of such data it is critical to identify which story-elements are being referred to at each time point of a participant’s recall. Currently, this task is typically performed by human annotators, a process which is effortful and susceptible to human error. We present our ongoing work on an LLM-based tool, available as a Python package and CLI, that automates this recall matching. Our tool achieved strong agreement with human annotators on written narratives, though performance on movie narratives was more variable. The tool also remained highly consistent in its ratings across repeated runs. By automating story-to-recall matching, this tool aims to facilitate naturalistic memory research while improving consistency and reproducibility.

submissions.title: Encoding models reveal selective differences in face representations in developmental prosopagnosia
submissions.abstract: People with developmental prosopagnosia (DP) struggle to recognize faces even though other aspects of their vision remain intact. This suggests that neural representations in DP are altered. Are these differences specific to the face-selective cortex and face stimuli, or a part of a broader visual processing deficit? To address this question we collected high-quality fMRI data from 7 neurotypical and 3 DP subjects and used ANN-based encoding models to test for differences in neural representations. We find that model prediction scores in the fusiform face area (FFA) were consistently lower in DPs than in NTs. This reduction was not explained by noisier data, as prediction scores in the body-selective extrastriate body area (EBA) were comparable across groups. Category-level analyses further showed that the reduction in FFA predictivity was specific to face images, with no group differences for bodies, scenes, or objects, and no face-specific deficit in EBA. Together, these findings point to selective differences in face representations in DPs in the FFA and show how ANN-based models can be used to characterize representational differences in the brain.

submissions.title: The hippocampus represents abstract graph structure at multiple scales along its longitudinal axis
submissions.abstract: Humans extract latent structure from their environment, and growing evidence suggests the hippocampus encodes such structure through predictive representations. In spatial domains, these representations are organized along the hippocampal longitudinal axis, with posterior regions encoding finer-grained, local structure and anterior regions supporting more global, coarse-grained structure. To test whether the same principle applies to abstract, non-spatial relational structures, we reanalysed fMRI data from participants viewing sequences drawn from a previously learned graph. We found that the left hippocampus represents abstract graph structure at multiple scales, with predictive scale increasing from posterior to anterior regions. Our findings suggest that hippocampal multi-scale predictive representations may be a domain-general mechanism for relational processing.

submissions.title: Separating Numerosity and Proportion Representations Through Pretraining
submissions.abstract: Numerosity and proportion are two fundamental types of quantitative information extracted from visual scenes, and both can be discriminated early in life. Although these cues are correlated in natural environments, incongruent combinations can occur. Young children can distinguish each individually but struggle when they conflict, suggesting that the neural representations supporting them are not yet fully refined. Here, we tested whether training on natural image classification alone can promote this refinement. We compared an untrained neural network with a network pre-trained on natural images and analyzed their latent representations. Pre-training increased the principal angle between subspaces and reduced interference in ablation analyses. Consistently, the pre-trained network showed higher accuracy in an interference task. These findings suggest that natural visual experience reorganizes quantitative representations into a more separable form.

submissions.title: Arousal Is the Odd One Out: Affective Properties Occupy a Unique Dimension in Human Object Representations
submissions.abstract: How are objects represented in the human mind? We analyze property ratings for 1,823 everyday objects from the THINGS database to characterize the latent structure of human conceptual space. Using principal component analysis and cross-property prediction, we find that most object properties - including physical, biological, and manipulability dimensions - form a tightly redundant representational structure captured by two principal components. Affective properties, particularly arousal, are a striking exception: arousal cannot be predicted from structural object properties (R2 = 0.32), placing it in a dimension largely orthogonal to the rest of conceptual space. These findings suggest that the human conceptual system organizes objects along two dissociable axes – a structural/physical axis and an affective axis – and raise questions about whether current computational models of object knowledge, which are typically trained on visual and linguistic statistics, capture the full dimensionality of human object representations.

submissions.title: Biologically Constrained Heterogeneity: Hybrid Spiking-Nonspiking Connectome-Constrained Models
submissions.abstract: In diverse neural circuits, ranging from the locust locomotor system to the mouse retina, information is processed through the coordinated activity of spiking and nonspiking neurons. Some research suggests a potential evolutionary benefit to this dual-modality processing, and cellular heterogeneity is known to enhance robust learning in spiking neural networks (SNNs). Current research on nonspiking neurons in biological contexts primarily focuses on the trade-offs between local and global signals. However, the specific contribution of graded versus action potential-mediated signal propagation has rarely been isolated and tested within connectome-constrained models. While precise cellular parameters are often difficult to obtain, the classification of a neuron as graded or action-potential based is often well-characterized (e.g., photoreceptors tend to be nonspiking across organisms, whereas higher-order levels of the visual system such as RGCs in vertebrates and LPTCs in Drosophila tend to be spiking). We exploit this known heterogeneity to investigate whether directly connected spiking-nonspiking hybrid architectures provide a computational edge. We first validate the viability and robustness of this architecture on an auditory spiking identification task, the Spiking Heidelberg dataset, and find that hybrid networks outperform homogeneous baselines most strongly under limited neurons or training data. We then demonstrate the viability of this framework in a connectome-constrained model of the Drosophila antennal lobe which achieves 93-95\% test accuracy when trained on a 200+ odor classification task. PCA of projection neuron activity in our model reveals greater linear separability in odor representations relative to other neuron types in the antennal lobe, consistent with biological findings. Together, these results establish hybrid spiking-nonspiking architectures as a promising alternative for spiking tasks.

submissions.title: Interfacing Macaque Cortex with Language Models for Generative Neural Readout
submissions.abstract: Recent advances in neural decoding have moved beyond categorical readouts toward richer, semantically grounded representations, for example by mapping brain activity elicited by natural scenes to language embeddings of image captions. While effective, such approaches remain limited to static representations. To enable more flexible and interactive decoding of neural data, recent work has proposed interfacing brain activity directly with large language models (LLMs), allowing neural signals to condition open-ended language generation. However, these approaches have so far been restricted to human fMRI and time-averaged signals. Here, we extend this approach to intracranial recordings from macaque visual cortex during passive viewing in the THINGS dataset. We show that time-resolved neural activity is decodable into natural language, enabling generative readout of visual content. These preliminary results demonstrate that LLM-based neural decoding interfaces generalize beyond human fMRI and suggest that language-compatible structure is present in non-human primate visual representations.

submissions.title: A Reproducibility Framework for Subject-Level Alzheimer’s Decoding
submissions.abstract: Many EEG papers warn about leakage, unstable validation, and weak reporting, yet these issues still appear frequently in current disease-classification studies (Brookshire et al., 2024; Kapoor & Narayanan, 2023; Kunjan et al., 2021). We make these risks concrete in one exemplar problem: Alzheimer's disease (AD) vs control (CN) decoding on OpenNeuro ds004504 (Miltiadous et al., 2023; Markiewicz et al., 2021). We evaluate three traps together, in one auditable workflow. Trap 1 (identity leakage): when epochs from the same subject appear in both train and test sets (subject-overlap), accuracy is inflated. Trap 2 (cohort sensitivity): even when no subject appears in both sets (subject-disjoint), results can still vary strongly depending on which subjects are held out. Trap 3 (objective mismatch): epoch-level metrics (an epoch is a short EEG segment treated as one sample) and subject-level metrics can rank models differently. To empirically demonstrate these traps, we compare PCA against a univariate T-test feature selector across KNN, SVM, XGBoost, and MLP. Overlap versus subject-disjoint splits test Trap 1, varying held-out cohort size and composition across repeated cohorts tests Trap 2, and epoch-versus-subject ranking comparisons test Trap 3. This work provides a reproducibility framework that makes leakage, cohort sensitivity, and objective mismatch jointly visible and testable. We recommend the use of subject-disjoint LOSO/LPSO (Leave-P-Subjects-Out) splits, reporting fold/cohort variability (SD), and reporting both epoch and subject accuracy.

submissions.title: Predicting Individualized Functional Topographies in Autism Spectrum Disorder
submissions.abstract: Functional localizers have been widely used to localize individualized functional areas. However, given constraints on scanning efficiency, ecological validity, and the practical challenges of collecting localizer data in clinical populations, alternative approaches are needed. Previous work has found that hyperalignment can estimate category-selective topographies with high fidelity, even in individuals with perceptual deficits such as face blindness. Here, we extend hyperalignment to individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), a developmental disorder with deficits in face perception and category-selective cortex. Using a dataset consisting of 24 individuals with ASD and 24 controls, we predicted their topographies for faces and objects using connectivity hyperalignment (CHA), and compared the predicted maps with estimations from their own functional localizer data. On average, the CHA-predicted maps were highly correlated with participants’ own topographies at both the whole-brain and fine-grained searchlight level. Hence, we show that category-selective topographies can be estimated with high fidelity using hyperalignment in clinical populations with widespread atypical neural responses.

submissions.title: Reaching for Emotion Regulation with Reachy Mini
submissions.abstract: Cognitive neuroscience models often lack ecological validity due to constrained laboratory environments and thus fail to generalize to real-world clinical deployments. To bridge this gap, we propose an extensible bedside companion utilizing the Reachy Mini robot. Our ultimate vision is an embodied system that holistically assesses patient physiological and cognitive-affective states, autonomously alerts medical personnel to anomalies, and improves clinical outcomes while serving as an 'ecological laboratory' for naturalistic data collection. As a foundational step toward this vision, this work establishes a core affective regulation loop. We continuously monitor a user's emotional state in unconstrained settings using Electroencephalography (EEG), video, and speech. Upon detecting negative emotional shifts, a Large Language Model (LLM) triggers targeted cognitive interventions: auditory stimuli (music), semantic information processing (news), a collaborative story-building game, and a targeted cognitive assessment: Montreal Cognitive Assessment-Blind. By continuously measuring responses during these tasks, the system closes the feedback loop to evaluate real-time emotion modulation. Ultimately, this demonstrates the viability of embodied AI for emotion regulation and real-world data capture.

submissions.title: Measuring Depth Inversion in the Ames Window Illusion
submissions.abstract:
How is the visual system able to resolve the ambiguity regarding depth and size of objects that results from the absence of binocular information?
    One angle that allows for the study of this phenomenon are illusions such as the rotating Ames Window, where an object appears inverted in depth for one half-cycle, resulting in an illusory oscillation. 
    We evaluate six modern depth estimation networks on their capability to reproduce this effect by measuring an object's estimated depth gradient over the course of one rotation. 
    We find that the depth gradient behaves in an oscillatory manner in all probed networks, suggesting some unifying commonality beyond network architecture.

submissions.title: Comparing Human and Machine Communication Patterns Through a Tangram Game
submissions.abstract: When humans communicate about visual objects, they develop shared linguistic conventions that progressively reduce referential ambiguity through collaborative dialogue. To test whether vision-capable large language models (VLLMs) exhibit similar communicative behaviors, we compare human-human and agent-agent interactions in the tangram communication game, where two players establish shared references for abstract shapes across six repeated rounds. We analyzed existing human-human data and conducted agent-agent experiments with five VLLMs, measuring performance and using representational probes to explore the structure underlying performance. Humans demonstrate clear convention formation, with representations becoming increasingly distinguishable as accuracy improves from 78\% to 96\%. In contrast, AI agents showed consistently low performance, typically around 10--30\%, with little evidence of convention development, despite access to conversation history, interim accuracy reports, and what appear to be largely accurate initial descriptions by ``director'' agents. These results suggest that current VLLMs may still struggle with grounded, evolving, coreferential communication in this collaborative setting.

submissions.title: Physical Stress Disrupts Maladaptive Emotion-Decision Loops in Depression with Non-Suicidal Self-Injury: Evidence from a Combinatorial Bandit Task
submissions.abstract: Non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) is a maladaptive coping behavior frequently co-occurring with major depressive disorder (MDD), yet the computational mechanisms underlying emotion--behavior dysregulation under stress remain unclear. Using a four-armed combinatorial bandit task with acute physical stress manipulation, we examined decision-making in healthy controls (HC, $n=48$), MDD patients with NSSI (NSSI$^+$, $n=43$), and those without (NSSI$^-$, $n=26$). Model-free analyses revealed a maladaptive emotion--behavior loop in MDD, characterized by lower performance and reduced affective sensitivity to positive feedback. In addition, stress increased suboptimal repetition of choice with low deterministic payoffs in NSSI$^+$. Computational modeling showed that MDD had lower learning rates and reduced exploration, with NSSI$^+$ also characterized by higher initial values and diminished directed exploration. Stress facilitated decay of selection history, and decay of values in NSSI$^-$. These findings delineate behavioral and computational signatures of NSSI in depression awaiting further consolidation.

submissions.title: Context-Dependent Relational Warping Underlies Triangle Inequality Violations in a Large Language Model
submissions.abstract:
Vector-space accounts assume that relational similarity is determined by fixed positions in a metric space, implying that
  similarity judgments should satisfy triangle inequality. Yet behavioral work has shown selective violations in mixed
  triangles, where the same ambiguous pair participates in different relations across comparisons. This raises a mechanistic
  question: how can a vector-based system produce context-dependent relational judgments if pair representations are fixed?
  We address this question in Llama-3.1-70B by comparing consistent and mixed triangles and by examining internal
  representations during in-context learning. The model reproduces the human asymmetry: triangle inequality is largely
  preserved in consistent triangles but systematically violated in mixed triangles. Internal analyses of condition-specific
  function vectors projected into a shared PCA space show that the ambiguous pair does not remain at a single stable
  location, but shifts toward different relation-specific directions as context changes. These findings suggest that mixed-
  triangle violations arise from context-sensitive representational warping, indicating that fixed-metric accounts are
  insufficient to explain relational similarity under changing context.

submissions.title: Hierarchical Organization of Actions in Creative Problem Solving: Evidence from the Puzzle Game Baba Is You
submissions.abstract: Real-world problem-solving requires creatively redefining constraints, a process captured by the rule-dynamic puzzle \textit{Baba Is You}. However, modeling human strategies in such open-ended environments faces significant computational challenges: state-action space explosion, researcher bias in "top-down" operator definitions, and the non-Markovian nature of latent subgoals. Here, we develop an objective, bottom-up framework to identify atomic operators (OPs) and cluster them into Functional Units (FUs), aligning with evidence that humans construct simplified mental representations to plan. Applying a 4-state Hidden Markov Model(HMM) on inter-move reaction times (RTs), we dissociate latent states of intensive deliberation to quantify planning depth. Analyzing $1.2$ million actions from $1,118$ participants, we show that deliberation peaks during low-motor-load navigation and at the starting point of complex subgoals. This temporal gap widens at higher levels of the abstraction hierarchy (OP $\to$ FU), suggesting a strategic front-loading of computational resources. Furthermore, significant shifts in operator distributions post-failure indicate that restarts trigger global re-evaluations of internal models. Our findings provide a data-driven account of how humans optimize hierarchical planning to navigate and restructure causal logic.

submissions.title: The Claw Machine Task: Modelling Confidence in Tool Use
submissions.abstract: Advanced tool use requires evaluating a range of uncertainties. We introduce the Claw Machine experimental paradigm, a novel tool-use task in which reward structure and outcome uncertainty are manipulated independently, eliciting separate confidence ratings for action selection and physical execution. Data are reported from a preliminary sample of 36 out of 40 planned participants. A Bayesian negative entropy model, parameterised by inverse temperature $\beta$ indexing the degree to which reward influences confidence, captures this dissociation: action selection confidence tracks expected utility and varies with reward structure, while execution confidence reflects object properties and outcome variability independently of reward. Model-fitted $\beta$ did not correlate significantly with independent risk-taking (BART), suggesting reward sensitivity in structured tasks may be dissociable from general risk tolerance under ambiguity.

submissions.title: Model manifold analysis suggests the human ventral visual system is less like an optimal classifier and more like a feature bank
submissions.abstract: What do deep neural network (DNN) models actually tell us about the computational principles of visual information-processing in the biological brain? A now common finding in visual neuroscience is that many different kinds of DNNs -- with different architectures, tasks, and training diets -- are all comparably performant predictors of image-evoked brain activity in the ventral visual cortex. This relative parity of diverse models may at first seem to undermine the common intuition that these models can be used to infer the computational principles that govern the visual brain. In this work, we show to the contrary that comparable brain-predictivity does not preclude the differentiation of these same models in terms of the underlying manifold geometries that define them. To do this, we assess 12 manifold geometry metrics computed on a diverse set of 117 DNN models, curated to include multiple tasks, architectures, and input diets. We then use these metrics to predict how well each model aligns with occipitotemporal cortex (OTC) activity from the human fMRI Natural Scenes Dataset. We find that *manifold signal-to-noise ratio* (a metric previously associated with few-shot learning) is a robust predictor of downstream brain-alignment and supersedes both other manifold geometry metrics (i.e. *manifold capacity*) and downstream task-performance (e.g. top-k recognition accuracy) across multiple image sets (e.g. ImageNet21K versus Places365) and controlled model comparisons (e.g. assessments across ImageNet-1K trained architectural variants only). These results add to a growing body of evidence that the ventral visual stream serves as a basis set (or feature vocabulary) for object recognition rather than as the actual locus of recognition *per se*.

submissions.title: Can Human Perceptual Similarity Alignment Improve Interpretability in Visual Representations?
submissions.abstract: What makes the features learned by vision models interpretable to humans? We introduce a psychophysics protocol that directly measures feature interpretability—the degree to which a person, given a feature visualization and importance maps, can predict where that feature will activate in a new image. The logic is simple: if a feature captures a recognizable visual concept, observers should be able to localize it; if it does not, they will struggle. Applying this protocol to sparse autoencoder features from a range of vision transformers, we find that self-supervised and foundation models are consistently less interpretable than their supervised counterparts. While fine-grained alignment with human similarity judgments is uniformly high across models and does not predict interpretability, coarse-grained alignment—capturing semantic rather than perceptual structure—is a stronger correlate, suggesting that further improvements in interpretability depend less on perceptual fidelity than on whether a model's representations reflect the semantic organization of human perception.

submissions.title: Optimal Retinal Ganglion Cell Allocation under Fixed Channel Budgets
submissions.abstract:
The mammalian retina must compress a high-dimensional visual scene into a limited number of retinal ganglion cell (RGC) spike trains along the optic nerve. Given the optical constraints of the eye lens, such as aberrations, input image statistics contain varying local spatial complexity around the fovea. Furthermore, the primate fovea dedicates 80\% of ganglion cells to the central visual field. We hypothesize that a nonuniform allocation is optimal from an information-theoretic perspective.
We model RGC distributions across retinal regions as a fixed-budget resource allocation problem and compare allocation strategies against rate-distortion theory. Our computational pipeline treats RGCs as mosaics of Difference-of-Gaussians (DoG) receptive fields tiled via $k$-means Voronoi cells, where each cell's center radius scales as $\sigma_c = s\sqrt{A_i}$ with its patch area $A_i$. Images are encoded into ON/OFF half-wave-rectified ganglion-cell responses and reconstructed via a minimum-norm matched-filter pseudoinverse decoder. Allocation strategies are compared against rate-distortion theory, which analytically predicts that optimal resources scale with $n_i \propto c_i^{1/(1+p)},$ where $c_i$ is local gradient-energy complexity and $p$ governs the distortion power law. We also test whether the optimal allocation is achievable under evolutionary algorithm schemes with random initializations. Experiments use synthetic image ensembles with controlled regional statistics---horizontal bands of varying texture and concentric foveal rings---and compare the uniform, gradient-energy optimal, and adversarial reverse cell allocations. Across all tested budgets ($N = 8 \sim 8192$), the gradient-energy optimal allocation consistently yields the lowest reconstruction MSE, with the benefit growing monotonically with both budget size and inter-regional complexity contrast. The reverse baseline consistently under-performs, confirming that allocation order matters. Evolutionary learning converges in the direction of the theoretically optimal allocation and ultimately surpasses it, achieving lower MSE than the analytic solution. Taken together, these results support the normative hypothesis that the primate fovea's disproportionate ganglion-cell density is consistent with complexity-matched, rate-distortion-optimal coding.

submissions.title: PyDDMBayes: A Multilevel Bayesian Framework for Generalized Drift-Diffusion Modeling
submissions.abstract: Generalized drift-diffusion models (GDDMs) extend the classical DDM to support richer mechanistic hypotheses about decision-making. Standard approaches fit participants independently or pool them entirely, forcing a trade-off: independent fits are noisy and data-hungry, while pooled fits obscure individual variation. Multilevel modeling can resolve this trade-off through partial pooling, but existing multilevel implementations are restricted to classical DDM forms or require computationally expensive pre-training for each GDDM. More fundamentally, bridging multilevel modeling with GDDMs poses statistical challenges that off-the-shelf solutions do not overcome. Here we present PyDDMBayes, a framework and Python toolbox for multilevel Bayesian analysis of arbitrary GDDMs. In simulation, multilevel estimation reduces participant-level parameter recovery error compared to unpooled maximum likelihood, particularly with few trials. We show how a single multilevel GDDM yields both population-level inference and participant-level estimates of individual differences, and how the framework supports model comparison between competing mechanisms. This framework unifies inference across levels of analysis for arbitrary GDDMs.

submissions.title: The aging of creative problem solving revealed by the dynamics of latent cognitive-behavioral states
submissions.abstract: Traditionally, aging declines are attributed to isolated capacity declines (e.g., executive function, fluid intelligence), but it remains unclear whether aging difference in creative problem-solving (CPS) primarily reflect impairments in specific cognitive capacities or declines in the dynamic coordination of cognitive processes, especially in open-ended, real-world-like situation. We addressed this using a novel, ecologically valid paradigm adapted from the dynamic puzzle game $\textit{Baba Is You}$. In two online experiments (121 younger, 114 older adults), older adults showed significantly poorer CPS performance despite comparable working memory and other core cognitive abilities. To uncover the mechanisms, we segmented variable-length behavioral logs (16–2150 actions), extracted temporal-spatial-interaction features, and applied Bayesian Hidden Markov Models (BHMM) to infer latent cognitive-behavioral states and their transitions. Information-theoretic analyses of these latent dynamics further showed that older adults exhibited longer segment duration normalized by the segment-wise perplexity of latent states, which partially mediated the age-related performance decline. These findings indicate that aging impairs CPS primarily through reduced flexibility in dynamically coordinating cognitive states, rather than deficits in isolated capacities. This computational framework provides new mechanistic insights into cognitive aging in complex problem solving.

submissions.title: An Optimal Compression Principle for Event Segmentation and Encoding
submissions.abstract: Humans spontaneously segment continuous experience into events, which shape memory and learning. Yet it remains unclear what objective or principle makes particular moments function as boundaries.  We propose an information-theoretical framework, Minimum Description Length (MDL), that accounts for behavioral boundaries in sequences of stimuli by balancing global coding simplicity against within-event accuracy. This principled approach optimizes compression to extract generalizable event schema from noisy experiences, producing a family of hierarchical segmentations controlled by one granularity parameter. Across naturalistic video and audio stimuli, MDL boundaries align with human segmentation judgments. In simulations, the same principle recovers latent event structure without hand-specified state priors; and captures the U-shaped curve of free recall. The MDL framework suggests that event boundaries may emerge from general pressure toward efficient representation.

submissions.title: Efficiency and noise processing in early visual system
submissions.abstract: The brain is known to perform active inference despite optic nerve constraint and noise. Earlier works have shown that noise can be beneficial under certain conditions. We use VAE as a model of the early visual system. Under a sparse prior, we find that noise can help efficient coding and observe emergence of bioplausible RFs and whitening as a result. Hence, we hypothesise that sparsity of neural code exists to exploit noise. Ongoing work solidifies this hypothesis.

submissions.title: Neural Typicality in Naturalistic fMRI Defines an Interpretable Representation for Clinical Classification
submissions.abstract:
Naturalistic paradigms evoke structured neural responses shared across individuals, providing a rich but high-dimensional signal for studying brain function. Translating this signal into clinically useful representations, however, remains challenging. Here, we use Neural Typicality (Ntyp), a voxelwise measure of alignment to a shared response during naturalistic movie viewing, to construct a compact representation of brain dynamics and apply it to diagnostic classification in people with multiple sclerosis (pwMS).

Using this representation, we achieve reliable classification of pwMS versus healthy controls using simple feature extraction strategies, with data-driven decomposition yielding the strongest performance. Permutation testing confirms that classification reflects true disease-related structure. This was consistent across multiple movies acquired in separate scanning sessions.

The dimensions driving classification correspond to coherent, bilaterally organized brain networks that can be projected back onto the cortex, demonstrating that predictive performance arises from structured, interpretable brain organization rather than a black-box model. The ability to inspect these networks directly links classification to interpretation.

Together, these results show that naturalistic neural alignment defines a compact and meaningful representation of brain function that enables classification while revealing the neural structure underlying group differences.

submissions.title: Dissociating different sources of uncertainty in mice
submissions.abstract: Adaptive decision-making requires representing uncertainty often about several latent variables. While previous studies suggest that animals might represent uncertainty, it remains unclear whether such representations extend beyond task-relevant decision variables to include auxiliary perceptual variables. Here, we test whether mice represent both perceptual and decision uncertainty in a Go/No-Go orientation discrimination task while recording from area V1. We independently manipulated decision uncertainty (via stimulus orientation) and perceptual uncertainty (via stimulus contrast and dispersion). We then developed a Bayesian ideal observer (BIO) model that estimates trial-wise posterior distributions over stimulus orientation and choice. The model, fit to individual mice, outperformed both stimulus-based and behavior-only baselines in predicting choices. Estimated posteriors revealed dissociable structure: decision uncertainty was more strongly modulated by orientation, while perceptual uncertainty was driven by contrast and dispersion. These results provide evidence that animals might track multiple sources of uncertainty, and establish a framework for linking behaviorally inferred uncertainty to neural population activity. This approach enables direct tests of whether and how cortical circuits encode uncertainty during complex decision-making.

submissions.title: Geometric Signatures of Event Boundaries in Brain Foundation Models
submissions.abstract: Brains segment continuous experience into discrete events at moments of prediction error. These boundaries shape what is remembered and how experiences are interpreted. We ask whether a resting-state fMRI foundation model can capture neural event structure during movie watching. Using SwiFT_v2, a pretrained resting-state fMRI foundation model, applied to StudyForrest (N=15, Forrest Gump, ~162 behavioral event boundaries), we find that event boundary information is not decodable per-timepoint but emerges when averaging across many boundaries as a significant increase in embedding distance (p=.0003). These transitions involve representational displacement (cosine, Procrustes distance significant) without restructuring (local dimensionality, effective rank null). Temporal autocorrelation drops at boundaries (p=.028), providing a direct prediction failure signature. Signals appear only in later transformer layers (p<.02), and cross-subject alignment decreases at boundaries (p<.001). Foundation model embeddings thus capture event structure as continuous geometric transitions, complementing HMM's discrete detection.

submissions.title: Towards a minimal model of early phonetic learning
submissions.abstract: We study the relationship between learning mechanisms and predicted developmental trajectories in early phonetic learning. We show that, when set up appropriately, a simple minibatch K-means algorithm correctly predicts the emergence of a cross-linguistic difference between American English- and Japanese-learning infants in the perception of English R vs L, as in “rock” vs. “lock.” These results contribute to the ongoing exploration of the constraints that developmental trajectories of phonetic perception place on the associated learning mechanisms.

submissions.title: Asymmetric Interruption Costs Reflect Transition Structure Shaped by Task-Neutral Attractors
submissions.abstract:
Unexpected interruptions lead to persistent performance costs in subsequent task execution. 
Within a dynamical systems framework of cognitive control, where task-specific states are 
represented as attractors, interruption costs can arise from changes in the local dynamics of 
existing attractors or from the introduction of task-neutral attractors that alter transition structure, 
changing the rate of convergence. We tested these hypotheses using behavioral experiments and computational modeling. 
Behaviorally, interruptions increased response times in an asymmetric manner: 
returning to the pre-interruption task incurred larger costs than switching to an alternative task. 
This asymmetry was captured only when the local dynamics were modulated via changes in 
recurrent gains combined with an additional task-neutral attractor. 
These results suggest that recovery from unexpected interruptions is governed by 
multiple neural mechanisms changing the overall energy landscape among task attractors.

submissions.title: Directional Confusions Reveal Inductive Bias Through Rate–Distortion Geometry
submissions.abstract:
Humans and modern vision models can reach similar classification 
accuracy while making systematically different kinds of mistakes — 
differing not in how often they err, but in who gets mistaken for 
whom, and in which direction. We show that these directional 
confusions reveal distinct inductive biases invisible to accuracy 
alone. Using matched human and deep vision model responses on a 
natural-image categorization task under 12 perturbation types, we 
quantify asymmetry in confusion matrices and link it to generalization 
geometry through a rate--distortion (RD) framework, characterized by 
slope (beta), curvature (kappa), and efficiency (AUC). Humans 
exhibit broad but weak asymmetries, whereas deep vision models show 
sparser, stronger directional collapses — a dissociation confirmed to 
be independent of accuracy. Robustness training reduces global 
asymmetry but fails to recover the human-like breadth--strength 
profile. Mechanistic simulations show that broad--weak and sink-like 
organizations produce opposite shifts in RD frontier geometry even 
when matched for performance, suggesting that human-aligned robustness 
requires redistributing error structure, not just reducing it.

submissions.title: Beyond shapshot vision: decoding dynamic videos  from temporally evolving neural activity
submissions.abstract: Visual perception requires processing of dynamic, continuously changing inputs, which elicit neural responses that unfold dynamically over time. Temporal dynamics of visual representations are extensively studied in the context of static vision, e.g. by testing how well visual images can be decoded from time-resolved human brain signals. Less is known about the temporal characteristics of neural responses to dynamic stimuli. Here, we directly compare the neural processing of static and dynamic inputs by computing temporal decoding profiles from electro-encephalography (EEG) activity measured in human subjects viewing short naturalistic videos and matched single-frame images. We ask the following questions: 1) Are dynamic videos and static images similarly decodable from EEG responses? 2) How well do neural representations generalize between images and videos? and 3) Is this generalization between formats modulated by video dynamics? We find that images and videos yield comparable within-format decoding accuracies at early stages of the EEG response time course, but videos are better decodable later in time (>200 ms). Neural decoding does substantially but not fully generalize across formats, with later convergence depending on the temporality of the video content. Specifically, image decoding generalizes least to highly temporal videos, suggesting that additional, video-specific representations are involved. These findings reveal unique neural representations for video over images.

submissions.title: The Baby Intuitions Benchmark 2: Evaluating Social Intelligence in Humans and Machines
submissions.abstract: Human actions are driven by both instrumental goals to effect change in the physical world and social goals to engage with others. Even young infants appear capable of recognizing and reasoning about these goals, supporting early learning about agents and their environment. Can advanced artificial intelligence reason about the instrumental and social goals of others? The Baby Intuitions Benchmark 2 (BIB2) is designed to test this question. We present BIB2 along with preliminary data from N = 64 adults, validating expected patterns of human performance. We further introduce two computational models to be evaluated on BIB2: (1) a video transformer model that has shown success on BIB2’s predecessor, the Baby Intuitions Benchmark; and (2) a variant that incorporates inductive biases for social learning via pretraining on SAYCam-S, a large, naturalistic dataset of head-mounted video from a single infant. By probing inference about affiliation and agency from minimal cues, BIB2 provides a principled framework for studying the foundations of social intelligence and for advancing human-like AI.

submissions.title: Beyond Averages: Identifying Latent Behavioral Strategies in Approach–Avoidance Conflict Using Probabilistic Clustering
submissions.abstract: Individuals differ in how they navigate approach–avoidance conflicts (AAC), balancing rewards and punishments. We applied Bayesian Gaussian mixture modeling to an AAC paradigm and identified three latent behavioral strategies: coarse value-sensitive explorers, cost–benefit optimizers, and non-avoiders. These clusters differed in how selectively participants allocated effort across reward–punishment conditions, revealing graded versus coarse or indiscriminate strategies. Our results highlight that adaptive and maladaptive avoidance arise from distinct mechanisms and that probabilistic clustering can uncover hidden behavioral heterogeneity with relevance for neural and clinical investigations.

submissions.title: Characterizing Decision Strategies from Think-Aloud in Risky Choice
submissions.abstract: Models of risky choice typically infer decision processes from gamble attributes and observed choices rather than directly observing the reasoning that unfolds during decision-making. Although such models can predict behavior well, their latent variables are researcher-specified, motivating interest in think-aloud protocols as a window into the human decision process. However, prior think-aloud work has often relied on either manual analysis that is difficult to scale or predictive use of language models that offers limited insight into reasoning structure. Here, we test whether think-aloud verbal reports can be distilled into interpretable representations that both reveal structure in reasoning and capture decision-relevant information that improves prediction of choice behavior. We compared baselines with think-aloud-based models ranging from interpretable abstractions of participants’ verbal reports to sanitized and full transcript representations. Think-aloud-based representations improved prediction over an LLM baseline that received only option values and probabilities, with progressively richer representations yielding higher accuracy. Some models that used abstract representations of think-aloud also outperformed the Expected Value and Prospect Theory baselines. These results suggest that think-aloud can be transformed into interpretable abstractions that reveal sequential reasoning structure and additional decision-relevant signal not captured by gamble attributes and observed choices alone. More broadly, this framework uses think-aloud to bridge formal models of choice with the reasoning processes that drive behavior.

submissions.title: Downsampled Representations Improve Cross-Model Transfer in hV4 Encoding-Model Metamers
submissions.abstract: Metamers are physically distinct images that produce the same response in a model or brain area and can therefore probe which image changes leave that response unchanged. In brain-response modeling, encoding models can synthesize images that preserve the predicted response to a reference image. However, matching a single fitted encoding model does not by itself support an inference about shared invariance within an ROI. We therefore define metamer validity as hold-out cross-model transfer to independently fit models not used during synthesis. Using hV4 responses from the Natural Scenes Dataset, we trained six AlexNet-based encoding models, reserving three for synthesis and three for hold-out evaluation. We varied the number of jointly matched synthesis models ($K=1,2,3$) and compared Pixel and Lowpass synthesis conditions. Hold-out transfer was consistently higher for Lowpass than for Pixel, and increases in $K$ produced more consistent gains in Lowpass than in Pixel. Thus, inferences from encoding-model metamers depend on both multi-model constraints and synthesis parameterization.

submissions.title: Dynamical systems analysis of a large-scale cortical language model enables mechanistic interpretation
submissions.abstract: The meanings of words and concepts arise in the brain as distributed cell assemblies spanning sensory and motor cortical areas. Understanding how such representations form and propagate across the cortical hierarchy is a central challenge for the cognitive neuroscience of language. Large-scale cortical models grounded in neuroanatomy provide a natural platform for this question, yet their complexity makes it difficult to relate observed dynamics to underlying circuit properties. We apply Wilson-Cowan mean-field theory and dynamical systems analysis to the MatCo model, a 12-area neural field model of language-related cortex, deriving analytical stability boundaries that partition parameter space into distinct dynamical regimes. We find that non-uniform sensory drive causes neurons within the same cell assembly to operate in different dynamical regimes, producing heterogeneous activity incompatible with a mean-field description. Normalising synaptic input resolves this, placing the assembly in a single, well-defined regime whose behaviour – from transient stimulus-driven responses to sustained reverberant activity – is accurately predicted by the analysis. Inter-areal propagation is governed by proximity to the saddle-node stability boundary: only near this boundary does recurrent amplification successfully recruit secondary and associative areas across different modalities, linking local excitatory-inhibitory balance to the conditions for distributed semantic memory retrieval. These results ground a complex cortical language model in dynamical systems theory, opening a principled path toward mechanistic accounts of language and meaning.

submissions.title: Bridging Encoding to Decoding: Synthetic fMRI from Brain Foundation Models Improves Neural Decoding
submissions.abstract: Encoding models predict brain activity from stimuli; decoding models invert this mapping—yet the knowledge accumulated in large-scale encoding models has not been leveraged for decoder training. Here we bridge them by using a brain encoding foundation model (TRIBE v2) to synthesize training data for decoder learning. We generate ~5,000 synthetic fMRI responses to natural images, align their distributions with real recordings through noise injection, and pretrain a visual decoder on this augmented set before finetuning on limited real data. This approach yields consistent improvements in retrieval-based decoding across all data regimes (28–42% relative gain, *p* < 0.05), and a shuffled-pairing control confirms that the gains arise from the encoding model's learned stimulus–brain mappings. These results demonstrate that knowledge accumulated in encoding foundation models can be transferred to decoding via synthetic data generation, offering a practical pathway to alleviate data constraints in neural decoding.

submissions.title: Adaptive Tuning of Human Learning to the Latent Structure of a Multi-Armed Bandit Task
submissions.abstract: Solving real-world decision-making tasks requires not only identifying optimal choices, but also adapting one’s search strategy to the structure of the learning environment. While generalisation and uncertainty-driven exploration have been shown to support learning in large, complex environments, it remains unclear whether and how humans adapt their search strategies to tasks with different latent reward structures. Here, we answer this question using multi-armed dynamic Bernoulli bandit tasks, comparing human search behaviour across spatially correlated and independent reward environments. We found that subjects learned to learn in both tasks and showed comparable meta-learning trajectories. Crucially, their patterns of exploration diverged with training, with participants in the independent tasks exploring less often but choosing farther away options and this was retained over days. Upon analysing subjects’ trial-by-trial behaviour through the lens of reinforcement learning (RL), we found that value generalisation over nearby options predicted participant choices in the correlated but not the independent task. Furthermore, models that incorporated a non-RL tendency to repeat previous choices better explained participant behaviour in the independent task but not in the correlated task. Together, our findings suggest that humans flexibly adapt their learning strategies to different task environments based on their latent correlation structure.

submissions.title: Predictive Latent Simulation as a Memory Retrieval Mechanism
submissions.abstract: Research on hippocampal sharp-wave ripples (SWR) suggests that memory retrieval and internal simulation are deeply intertwined: prospective sequences emerge during the same neural events that drive memory access, and their content reflects expected future relevance rather than recency. Yet the computational mechanism coupling imagination to retrieval remains underspecified. We propose that imagination-guided retrieval, using internally generated latent simulations as queries against stored experience, offers a parsimonious account of this coupling. We examine navigation agents that use a world model to imagine future states that index persistent memory, without those states ever being directly observable. Perfect-retrieval experiments across three navigation backbones reveal a consistent $\sim$20-point performance gap that localizes the bottleneck to simulation quality, and multi-agent memory sharing improves navigation in proportion to the agent pool, paralleling hippocampal replay reorganized by social observation. Together, these findings offer testable predictions for the imagination-retrieval hypothesis.

submissions.title: Do Better Visual Question Answering Models Attend More Like Humans?
submissions.abstract: We examine whether improvements in visual question answering (VQA) models are associated with more human-like attention behavior. Using the VQA-HAT dataset, which provides human attention annotations, we analyze the attention patterns of a state-of-the-art model (ViLT-B/32) and compare them with both human attention and prior VQA models. While the model achieves strong task performance, its attention alignment with human annotations remains substantially below human-human agreement and comparable to earlier architectures. These observations indicate that advances in model performance do not necessarily correspond to more human-like inductive biases in attention. These results suggest a fundamental dissociation between predictive accuracy and cognitive plausibility, challenging the assumption that architectural progress yields more human-like reasoning.

submissions.title: Anatomy-Aware Masked Image Modeling for Self-Supervised Learning on 3D Brain MRI
submissions.abstract: Self-supervised pre-training on structural brain MRI can learn transferable representations without diagnostic labels, but standard masked image modeling (MIM) masks patches uniformly at random, ignoring the brain's anatomical organization. Scattered patch reconstruction can be solved from local intensity cues alone, bypassing the inter-regional reasoning most relevant to neuropsychiatric conditions. We propose \textbf{anatomy-aware MIM}, which replaces random patch masking with region-level masking derived from cortical parcellations (\texttt{aparc+aseg}). By masking entire anatomical regions at a time, the encoder is forced to reconstruct missing brain structures from long-range inter-regional context rather than local neighborhoods, with no additional supervision or parameters. Integrated into a multi-task pre-training framework based on 3D Swin Transformer and evaluated via linear probing, anatomy-aware MIM improves schizophrenia classification over random MIM: balanced accuracy from 64.7\% to 66.9\%, AUC from 0.767 to 0.771, and recall from 0.398 to 0.451 (+13.3\% relative). These results support a broader principle that domain-appropriate masking is a meaningful inductive bias for self-supervised learning in structured biological systems.

submissions.title: Computational Natural Language Analysis Reveals Psilocybin-Induced Changes in Meaning-Making
submissions.abstract: Emerging evidence indicates that psilocybin produces sustained improvements in wellbeing, thought to be mediated by changes in how individuals construct meaning from internal and external experience. However, the mechanistic basis of this process is poorly understood. We draw on Linguistic Active Inference Theory (Yao, 2025) and the REBUS model (Carhart-Harris & Friston, 2019), to argue that naturalistic speech provides a tractable window into psychedelic-induced perturbations of precision weighting. Within this framework, psilocybin is hypothesised to reduce the precision of high-level prior beliefs, increasing sensitivity to incoming prediction errors and promoting more flexible inference. We tested this account in a sample of 40 healthy participants undergoing a single high-dose psilocybin intervention. Meaning-making dynamics were assessed via naturalistic thought sampling across 10 days both pre- and post-intervention, with speech data analysed using bag-of-words, probabilistic topic modelling and graph-based semantic network analyses. Psilocybin was associated with an increased frequency of self-referential and meaning-making terms. Graph-based analyses revealed reduced modularity and increased global integration within semantic networks — a pattern we interpret as reflecting reduced top-down prior precision and more flexible integration of information. These computational signatures were associated with a shift in inner speech valence towards more positive and regulatory forms, and increased wellbeing, supporting a mechanistic account linking psychedelic-induced precision modulation to psychological outcomes.

submissions.title: re:vision – A community-driven replication initiative for condition-rich neuroscience of visually-presented stimuli
submissions.abstract:
Condition-rich fMRI studies have contributed strongly to our understanding of visual representations in the brain and their alignment with deep neural networks. However, the datasets underlying these studies often capture only a fraction of visual experience or may undersample important parts of the visual world. This raises questions about the replicability and generalizability of these findings.
To address this challenge, we introduce re:vision, a community-driven initiative that aims to systematically replicate influential findings in the neuroscience of visually presented images to determine the degree to which the field reflects genuine findings beyond dataset-specific biases. re:vision is built on LAION-fMRI, a new multi-echo 7T fMRI dataset in which, over >30 sessions, five participants each viewed approximately 7,000 images selected to maximize coverage of visual and semantic space. In re:vision, researchers will replicate published studies following original analysis procedures as closely as possible. Beyond replication, the initiative aims to test generalization using out-of-distribution images and semantically defined subsets of the stimulus space. Through large-scale collaborative replication on a carefully constructed dataset, re:vision aims to establish a stronger empirical foundation for visual neuroscience and NeuroAI.

submissions.title: Recent Trial History Improves Encoding Models of Brain Responses During Emotional Video Viewing
submissions.abstract: Trial-wise brain responses during naturalistic viewing may depend not only on features of the current trial but also on recent stimulus history. Here, we investigated whether adding recent-trial information improves region-wise encoding models of trial-wise fMRI responses during emotional video viewing. Focusing primarily on emotion features, we compared current-only models with history-augmented models that incorporated 1-back and 2-back information, while also examining visual feature spaces in parallel. Adding 1-back features improved prediction across much of cortex and many subcortical regions, with the strongest gains observed for emotion features. Visual feature spaces also showed positive 1-back gains, but these were smaller. By contrast, adding 2-back features produced little further improvement beyond the 1-back model. These results indicate that trial-wise responses during emotional video viewing are not fully captured by current-trial features alone and that the most useful recent-history information is concentrated in the immediately preceding trial, particularly in the emotion feature space.

submissions.title: How RNNs shape the geometry of mixture inputs? Biased suppression and emergent codes stem from connectivity
submissions.abstract:
Neural circuits routinely process mixtures --- weighted combinations of simpler inputs.
Examples include plaids in vision, competing speakers in audition, odor blends in olfaction.
Empirically, the response to such mixtures can either combine the component responses proportionally,
or suppress one in favor of the other, or encode new directions that neither component alone produces \citep{Rust2006,Busse2009,Zoccolan2005}.
Which circuit properties determine which encoding arises?
The Divisive Normalization model captures the phenomenology of proportional and suppressive regimes,
but does not explain the underlying mechanisms, nor does it predict emergent mixture-selective directions.

This study shows how all three encoding geometries arise from a single mechanism in a biologically plausible network model: recurrent connectivity amplifies different directions of activity non-uniformly.
A mixture input shifts the network's operating point relative to each single stimulus, and this shift rescales each dynamical mode by a different factor.
Depending on the connectivity structure, this non-uniform rescaling can bias the mixture response toward one component or generate new encoding directions not reducible to any combination of single-stimulus responses.

Thus, in recurrent networks, the same stimulus family can be linearly mixed, selected, or segregated in the encoding space,
and this geometry can flexibly change with the stimulus itself. Mixture processing is a non-trivial computation, which has implications for downstream systems.

submissions.title: Adaptive Distortions of Confidence Reflect Environment Statistics and Internal Constraints
submissions.abstract: Confidence judgements are widely modelled as reflecting the strength of internal evidence, yet this account rests on SDT frameworks that assume static, symmetric decision environments. Although evidence reliability and natural input statistics can independently bias confidence (Boldt et al., 2017; Webb et al., 2023), how category priors and evidence variance jointly distort confidence towards accuracy correspondence remains unknown. Here, we manipulate category priors and evidence variance in SDT simulations while holding d’ constant. Skewed priors shift the decision criterion towards the frequent category, producing category-specific distortions in metacognitive sensitivity (AUROC2) without altering discrimination performance. Feedforward neural networks trained on MNIST digits and Gabor patches under unbalanced category frequencies develop the same asymmetric confidence patterns while maintaining classification accuracy, demonstrating that these distortions can emerge from optimisation dynamics alone, without explicit criterion computation. Our findings indicate that metacognitive precision is jointly shaped by environmental statistics and decision-policy optimisation.

submissions.title: A Modular Framework for Embedding Brain-like Topology in Recurrent Neural Networks
submissions.abstract: Spatially embedded recurrent neural networks (seRNNs) provide a framework for investigating how the brain’s spatial organisation shapes computation. Previous work extended this framework to include topological constraints, using the Earth Mover’s Distance between communicability distributions to drive artificial networks toward brain-like connectivity structure. A proof of concept demonstrated that such networks not only converge toward empirical communicability distributions but also develop spatially structured mixed selectivity for distinct cognitive demands — a functional signature absent in unconstrained networks. However, this initial demonstration required manual tuning and was limited to a single topological measure and task. Here we present a modular framework designed for the systematic investigation of how different structural properties of biological neural networks affect learning and computation. We present functional results from the original proof of concept, describe the framework’s design, and discuss how this approach enables controlled investigation of which topological properties of the brain matter for which computations.

submissions.title: Signal-to-Noise Ratio Predicts Neural Response Predictability with Limited Association with Tuning Properties in Mouse Visual Cortex
submissions.abstract:
What determines whether a neuron's activity can be accurately predicted 
by a deep neural network (DNN)? The field commonly assumes that neurons 
with strong, reliable responses are the most predictable. Here, we 
challenge this assumption by dissecting neural responses into signal and 
noise components using large-scale calcium imaging data from mouse visual 
cortex ($N = 78,853$ neurons). Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR; Spearman 
$\rho = 0.552$), rather than total response power ($\rho = 0.310$), is 
the dominant predictor of DNN prediction performance (trial-averaged 
correlation). Furthermore, we identify a population of neurons with high 
trial-to-trial variability but high signal power that achieves superior 
comparable predictability (mean performance $0.401$), challenging the view that high 
variability necessarily degrades encoding fidelity. This work establishes 
SNR as a principled metric for neuron selection in neural encoding 
models.

submissions.title: Belief Filtering: Meta-inference of Internal Models
submissions.abstract: Characterising the internal states underlying behaviour is challenging.  Human participants or other "agents" may act rationally, but with beliefs shaped by mistaken models of the causal structure of the environment and by internal noise.  External "observers" may access a veridical world state and witness behaviour, but have no direct view of beliefs, noise, or the internal model that shapes them.  Here, we demonstrate a formal framework to clearly distinguish agent and observer models, and their belief states, within an amortised meta-inference approach.  The approach makes it possible to track the evolution of an agent's beliefs across time, and thus identify the internal model on which it acts.

submissions.title: Spatial uncertainty underlies geometric distortions in navigation and grid cell tuning
submissions.abstract:
Navigation requires estimating one’s location from noisy sensory inputs. While environmental geometry is known to distort both navigational behavior and grid cell responses, these effects have been explained piecemeal. Here we propose a unifying principle: the brain maintains and updates uncertainty about spatial location, and this uncertainty shapes both behavior and neural coding.

We introduce the Bayesian Image-computable Observer for Navigation (BION) that integrates visual and self-motion inputs to infer a posterior over location. Crucially, spatial uncertainty is structured by environmental geometry due to retinal projection, yielding systematic inhomogeneities in information. These in turn explain human homing across trapezoidal, stretched, and compressed
environments. 

We further show that encoding this uncertainty in neural population codes predicts rat grid field size, anisotropy, rescaling, and boundary-tethering under analogous manipula-
tions. Unlike prior models that treat distortions as epiphenomena, our framework interprets them as optimal adaptations to uncertainty.

These results suggest that spatial uncertainty is not incidental but fundamental to navigation, providing a normative account linking perception, behavior, and neural representation.

submissions.title: Experienced dimensions of 3D scene structure provide organizing dimensions for scene-selective areas in the human brain
submissions.abstract: Here, we explore how natural visual experience of scenes is related to the representation of 3D scene structure in the human brain. First, we define a model to quantify 3D scene structure in terms of the distribution of surface normals and distances in arbitrary images. To quantify natural visual experience of these 3D structural features, we apply this model to samples of egocentric video frames drawn from a large database of head-mounted video collected while human subjects performed natural tasks. We then use principal components analysis to discover commonly experienced patterns of 3D structural features. We find that the first dimension of variance in scene structure distinguishes open from closed scenes. To relate visual experience of structure to brain responses, we model brain responses in the Natural Scenes Dataset as a function of the same 3D structural features. Analysis of fit model weights reveals a gradient of selectivity from open to closed scenes across multiple scene-selective areas. Thus, the main dimension that varies in our visual experience of scenes is mapped across scene-selective areas in the human brain.

submissions.title: Sensorimotor context modulates reinforcement learning
submissions.abstract: Reinforcement learning, a framework for human learning and decision-making, is influenced by a wide array of factors. One underexplored domain is sensorimotor context. This study examined behavior on a two-choice reversal learning task under two conditions: stationary (arm movements between parallel computers) and active (walking between computers). Participants chose repeatedly between two options rewarding at 70% and 30% probability, with the advantageous option reversing with 20% probability every 15 trials. A mixed-effects model revealed that sensorimotor context modulated reinforcement learning, but only in participants who completed the active condition first: the probability of repeating the same choice was higher in the subsequent stationary trials. No such effect emerged in the stationary-first group. Further work will use computational modeling, affective states, and strategy reports to identify the specific mechanisms.

submissions.title: Mode-Selective Memory Decay from Multilayer Neural Architecture: A Spectral Theory
submissions.abstract: Detailed episodic memories decay faster than schematic representations across behavioral, neuroimaging, and lesion paradigms, yet no formal model derives this rate separation from neural architecture. Complementary learning systems theory explains where fast and slow memories reside but not why their decay rates differ quantitatively. Spaced repetition models fit forgetting curves empirically but lack a mechanistic substrate. This paper introduces a spectral framework that formalizes memory as controlled state evolution on a product cognitive manifold equipped with a multilayer graph Laplacian. The Kronecker-sum structure of this Laplacian yields an additive eigenvalue decomposition in which high-frequency modes (encoding fine-grained perceptual detail) decay exponentially faster than low-frequency modes (encoding broad relational structure). The spectral gap of the weakest layer sets the global forgetting rate, producing a layer-bottleneck principle. A stability bound constrains how strongly intervention can perturb the system before reconsolidation-like overwrite occurs. Each operator component maps onto identified neural mechanisms, including hippocampal binding, neocortical consolidation, thalamic gating, and amygdala salience tagging. The framework predicts mode-selective decay, layer bottlenecking, load-sensitive forgetting, and reconsolidation margin violation, all of which align with established empirical findings. The Weibull forgetting curve emerges naturally as a consequence of multi-mode projection, and the spectral gap bounds the mutual information decay rate between the current and initial cognitive state. Preliminary validation from a deployed adaptive learning plat33 form (1,500+ users, 4,200 review events) supports the derived relationship between knowledge-graph spectral gap and observed retention (r=0.71, p<0.001). These results suggest that the detail-before-schema decay ordering is not an empirical regularity requiring fitting but a mathematical consequence of multilayer architecture, opening a path toward spectral methods as a unifying formalism across behavioral and neural levels of memory analysis.

submissions.title: CogMaze: A Benchmark of Egocentric Spatial Understanding in Humans and Vision-Language Models
submissions.abstract: Humans are adept at spatial understanding: integrating egocentric observations to support navigation and reasoning. Evidence suggests this relies on an allocentric representation of the environment (cognitive maps). While vision-language models (VLMs) perform well on many multimodal tasks, they remain weak at spatial understanding, suggesting they don't form cognitive map-like representations. We introduce CogMaze, a benchmark of spatial understanding in humans and VLMs. It includes a 3D simulated maze with visual landmarks, a ground-truth schema for probing representations, and tasks for humans and VLMs. We evaluate with a VLM in environments of varying complexity.

submissions.title: Human Causal Reasoning Demonstrates Neurosymbolic Structure in Exploration-driven Benchmarks
submissions.abstract: Studying how humans navigate sparse-reward environments may reveal architectural principles for more flexible AI, as human cognition excels where AI systems continue to struggle: in causal inference, learning from sparse data, and flexible problem-solving. To investigate this, 40 participants solved two instruction-less puzzle benchmarks with five levels each. Verbal reasoning traces were elicited using a think-aloud protocol; keystrokes, timestamps, and game states were logged as participants navigated the puzzles. Through grounded theory analysis of behavioral observations, verbal markers were tracked across trajectories of mechanic-based and objective-based learning, and then classified into a taxonomy of knowledge acquisition using natural language processing for feature extraction. Findings reveal the structured inferential processes of human learning, challenging the sufficiency of the traditional explore-exploit framework and motivating neurosymbolic architectures capable of genuine causal learning in sparse-reward, exploration-driven environments. We introduce 'establish' as a novel intermediary mechanism capturing the hypothesis-testing and confirmatory behaviors that bridge exploration and exploitation in computational learning models.

submissions.title: Meta-learning In-Context Enables Training-Free Cross Subject Decoding of Vision and Motor
submissions.abstract: Decoding neural representations across both visual and motor domains is fundamentally constrained by structural and functional inter-subject variability. Current methodologies typically require subject-specific training or gradient-based fine-tuning to account for individualized cortical organization. To address this limitation, we propose a meta-learning in-context framework that enables training-free cross-subject decoding. The model operates through a hierarchical inference process. First, it performs system identification by conditioning on a limited set of paired behavioral and neural data from a target individual, inferring voxel-specific forward encoding models. Second, the architecture aggregates these estimated encoder weights alongside observed neural activations across distributed cortical regions to execute functional inversion. This formulation predicts unseen visual stimuli and motor targets for novel subjects without requiring parametric updates, anatomical coregistration, or shared calibration datasets. By framing neural translation as an in-context learning objective, this approach demonstrates how generalized inverse models can scale across heterogeneous neural datasets and diverse sensorimotor applications.

submissions.title: Escape Response Reveals Computations Of Network Robustness
submissions.abstract: Whole-brain imaging in C. elegans with optogenetic stimulation of a few neurons that induce the escape response provides a comprehensive understanding of how the network achieves this robust behavior. With the advent of high-speed calcium imaging through Bessel illumination, we demonstrate that neurons with earliest onsets are not necessarily those directly anatomically connected to simulated neurons.

submissions.title: Geometric regularization of representation spaces enables efficient application of cognitive operators
submissions.abstract:
Humans solve many cognitive tasks by applying operators to internal representations rather than directly manipulating sensory input. A central challenge for artificial agents is to reach human-level generalization on abstract problems. One idea is to learn latent representation spaces whose geometric structure supports the efficient learning, application and generalization of operators \citep{marchetti2023equivariant, van2020plannable}. We refer to this kind of operator as a cognitive operator.
In this work, we study how the curvature of representation spaces influences the learnability and accuracy of cognitive operators corresponding to structured environmental transformations. Focusing on the mental rotation task, we model an agent using an encoder whose latent space serves as an internal representation. Drawing on tools from differential geometry, we formalize environmental transformations as Lie group actions and cognitive operators as vector fields on a latent manifold. Motivated by curvature-dependent error bounds for differential equations on Riemannian manifolds, we propose a set of curvature-regularization objectives that encourage locally linear, low-curvature latent geometries.
Experimental results on synthetic mental rotation stimuli show that curvature-regularized latent spaces yield more accurate operator learning performance. Together, these findings highlight the importance of latent geometry for bridging representation learning and cognitive computation, and provide a principled framework for learning cognitive operators in neural systems.

submissions.title: Understanding and Optimizing Contrastive Hebbian Learning Through Dynamical System Analysis
submissions.abstract: Contrastive Hebbian Learning (CHL), a dynamical system algorithm inspired from Hebb’s Rule, neurons that fire together wire together, is a local rule that requires no global feedback and aligns with brain inspired networks. Current implementations rely on fixed settling steps for integration to reach equilibrium. In this work we investigate the dynamical system of CHL to provide an objective method for quantifying settling time. By analyzing the layers trajectories, we can demonstrate that the network behaves as a stable linear differential equation with hidden layers converging to stable nodes, which can be analyzed mathematically. By quantifying the number of steps, we can show using CIFAR-10 and MNIST that we can provide a control mechanism for cutting training time iterations compared to fixed steps CHL models.

submissions.title: Interactions Between Features and Conjunctions during Category Learning
submissions.abstract: In learning multi-feature categories, humans often rely on primary features themselves rather than conjunction of these features. Conjunctions have also been recognized as critical for learning complex tasks, as conjunctions can expand the dimensionality of neural representations to allow for linear classification of categories which are nonlinear in the primary features (e.g. XOR). When humans learn a task requiring use of both feature and conjunctive information, it remains unclear how feature and conjunctive contributions to choice behavior interact across the learning trajectory.
